lesson.title: Multiple Inheritance: Combining More Than One Parent
lesson.summary: Multiple inheritance lets a Python class inherit from more than one parent class at once, gaining the attributes and methods of every parent, which is useful for combining independent capabilities but also introduces new questions about which parent's method wins if they conflict.
lesson.body:
Every inheritance example so far has used a single parent class. Python does not actually require that limitation. A class can list more than one parent class in its definition, separated by commas, and it will inherit from every single one of them at once. This is called multiple inheritance, and it is a feature many other object-oriented languages deliberately leave out, precisely because of the complications it can introduce, complications this section and the next will walk through carefully.

```python
class Flyer:
    def fly(self):
        return "Flying high."

class Swimmer:
    def swim(self):
        return "Swimming fast."

class Duck(Flyer, Swimmer):
    pass

d = Duck()
print(d.fly())
print(d.swim())
print(Duck.__mro__)
```

This prints `Flying high.`, then `Swimming fast.`, then a tuple: `(<class '__main__.Duck'>, <class '__main__.Flyer'>, <class '__main__.Swimmer'>, <class 'object'>)`. Duck defines nothing of its own at all, yet it gets full working access to both `fly`, from Flyer, and `swim`, from Swimmer, at the same time. Recall the is-a relationship from earlier in this unit: by inheriting from both, Duck is claiming to be a Flyer and to be a Swimmer, simultaneously, which fits a real duck rather well. Multiple inheritance is often used this way in Python, to combine several small, focused, independent classes, sometimes called mixins, into one richer class.

The trickier question is what happens when two parent classes define a method with the exact same name. If both Flyer and Swimmer had defined a method called `move`, which one would `d.move()` actually run? Python cannot answer that by relying on programmer intuition alone, it needs one single, precisely defined search order that it follows every time, for every class, without exception. That printed `__mro__` tuple in the example above is exactly that search order, listed out. Understanding exactly how Python builds that order, and how to reason about it confidently even in more tangled inheritance structures, is the focus of the final section in this unit: method resolution order.
